Autonomous Quadcopter Drone · Project · Oct 2024 – Mar 2025

An autonomous quadcopter that navigates, sees and decides.

From a bare frame to a drone that flies GPS waypoints, reads the world with OpenCV and makes its own decisions. It is built around a Pixhawk flight controller and a Raspberry Pi, with the code, design images and report open on GitHub. This page explains every layer, step by step: drag the 3D drone, tap its parts, run the demos.

Control · stabilisation

How a quadcopter flies

Two propellers spin clockwise and two counter-clockwise so their twisting forces cancel. Changing the speed of each motor independently makes the drone climb, tilt or turn.

Four controls, four motors
  • Throttle: all motors faster = climb.
  • Pitch: rear motors faster than front = nose tilts down and drone moves forward.
  • Roll: motors on one side faster = bank and move sideways.
  • Yaw: CW and CCW pairs differ = the drone rotates.

The sensors that tell it which way is up

Why control matters: stabilisation loop

A gust hits at t = 1 s. Without control the drone keeps tilting. A feedback controller (proportional + derivative, the core of a flight controller's rate loop) pushes back. Tune it.

Orange: no controller. Blue: with controller. Too little gain = slow recovery; too much Kd or Kp changes how sharp and twitchy the response is. Real tuning is done in flight tests. This is a simplified single-axis model for illustration.

How materials were chosen

Weight, strength, durability, cost, availability and environmental factors (temperature, humidity). The goal: light enough to fly long, tough enough to survive rough landings. The design follows an X-frame for simplicity and stability.

Mechanism · payload

The gripper that releases a fragile payload gently

A cam-driven, three-jaw gripper turned by a small servo. A 60° cam rotation closes the jaws; rotating back opens them. Springs act as dampers so the release is slow, not a jerk.

Drag to orbit

Parts
  • Base and top stand (structure)
  • 3 curved jaws, hinged to the base
  • Cam on the servo shaft (SG90)
  • 3 springs for controlled force
  • Rubber/silicone grip on jaw faces

Driving the servo from the Raspberry Pi

The repository's servo_controller.py uses 50 Hz PWM on GPIO 18. A servo reads the pulse width: a short pulse turns it one way, a long pulse the other. The code holds 7.5 % (locked) and switches to 12 % to release.

pulse width = duty ÷ 100 × 20 ms   ·   angle ≈ (duty − 2.5) ÷ 10 × 180°

In the repository How data leaves the drone

After decoding, data_sender.py posts a small package to a Flask receiver running on the ground laptop. The receiver prints it, saves the image and logs it. Press Send, then switch the network off and send again: the failure is logged and the mission continues.

In the repository The same idea as ROS 2

A ROS 2 node splits the work into separate programs: a camera node publishes frames on /camera/image_raw; qr_node subscribes, detects and decodes the QR code, and publishes the text on /qr_data. Any other node (navigation, logging, a dashboard) can then use it. This is the modular direction named in the README's future work.

Navigation & decision-making

How the drone finds its way

Autonomous navigation answers three questions: where am I, where do I want to go, and how do I get there safely? Position comes from GPS (and from mapping in unknown places), the route comes from a planner, and the decisions come from rules that handle surprises.

In the repository GPS waypoint navigation

goto_location() sends a latitude, longitude and altitude to the Pixhawk, then measures the haversine distance (distance along the Earth's curved surface) once per second. When the drone is within 1.5 m, the waypoint counts as reached. Set a target offset and run it.

Press the button to see the log the code prints.
a = sin²(Δlat/2) + cos(lat₁)·cos(lat₂)·sin²(Δlon/2)   d = 6371000 · 2 · asin(√a)

Explainer Path planning: choosing the route

A straight line is fine in open sky. With obstacles, the drone needs a planner. A* searches outward from the start, always expanding the cell that looks cheapest in total (cost so far plus estimated cost to go). Draw walls with your finger or mouse and press Find path.

Draw walls, then press Find path.

Green start, yellow goal, blue cells examined, orange final path.

Explainer SLAM: mapping while localising

GPS does not work indoors or under cover. SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) lets a robot build a map of an unknown place while working out where it is inside that map. A range sensor sends 48 rays; each ray marks free space along its length and an obstacle where it stops. Play it, then add pose drift: small position errors smear the map. Real SLAM fights this by matching new scans to the existing map and correcting at loop closures.

In the repository Real-time decision-making

Gates
Pre-flight checks stop the mission if there is no 3D GPS fix, the battery is under 10.5 V or the estimator is unhealthy.
Conditions
Altitude must reach 95 % of target; the waypoint counts only inside 1.5 m.
Timeouts & fallbacks
Scanning stops after 30 s and a safe default value keeps the mission moving.
Fail-safes
Any error or operator interrupt switches to return-to-launch, and resources are always released.
Computer vision · OpenCV

Giving the drone eyes

In the repository The Raspberry Pi reads frames from a camera with OpenCV and decodes QR codes in real time. Tap each stage of qr_scanner.py:

Real detection results

def _decode_frame(self, frame):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    gray = cv2.equalizeHist(gray)          # help in low light
    for barcode in pyzbar.decode(gray):
        if barcode.type == "QRCODE":
            return barcode.data.decode("utf-8")
    return None

Explainer Detection vs tracking

Detection runs on every frame and can jitter or miss. Tracking links detections over time, smooths the box and predicts where the target goes next. Both matter for moving targets and for keeping a drone locked on during landing.

A visual demonstration of the idea, not output from a trained model.

Explainer From perception to a decision

Environmental perception means turning sensor data into something the planner can use. With a depth camera, every pixel becomes a distance. The drone checks the corridor ahead; if something is inside its safety distance it chooses the free side. Move the obstacle.

Control · trajectory tracking

Following a path accurately

In the repository The Pi puts the Pixhawk in GUIDED mode and sends targets; the Pixhawk's own loops (position, attitude and rate, each faster than the one above) keep the drone stable and chase the target. Explainer Below, a drone must follow a moving reference. A stronger position gain tracks more tightly; wind pushes it away. Try it.

Orange dot: reference. White dot: drone. Simplified 2D model for illustration.

Outer loop: position
Compares where the drone is with where it should be and asks for a tilt.
Middle loop: attitude
Turns the requested tilt into the angles the airframe must hold.
Inner loop: rate
Fastest loop; uses the gyros to correct wobble and sets each motor.
Validation · simulate first

Prove it on a computer before it flies

Explainer A crash costs time, money and safety. So control and navigation are validated step by step, each stage cheaper and safer than the next. Model-based tools such as MATLAB and Simulink are used for the first stages; In the repository config.py also lists a simulator connection (SITL) so the same mission code can run before any flight. Tap each stage.

What simulation catches
Unstable gains, wrong signs, slow responses, logic bugs and unsafe edge cases.
What only flight shows
Real vibration, sensor noise, wind, battery sag and electromagnetic interference.

Testing · analysis

Do the numbers work?

Choosing parts is calculation first, testing second. Try the same two calculations I used to size the motors and battery.

Thrust needed

Total thrust: 4.74 kg

Per motor: 1.19 kg. The 2212 920 KV with 9.4×5.0 propellers was chosen to meet this.

Flight time estimate

Estimated flight time: 7.26 min

Time = capacity × 0.80 usable ÷ (current × 1000) × 60

Why a low-KV motor for a 450 mm frame?

Frame sizePropellerMotorKV
150 mm or smaller3 in or smaller1306 or smaller3000 KV or higher
250 mm6 in2204–22082000–2300 KV
350 mm7 in22081600 KV
450 mm (mine)8/9/10 in2212 or larger1000 KV or lower

Bigger frames use bigger, slower-spinning propellers: more efficient, so longer endurance.
